title: Safety envelope for KV demotion with continuous batching probes
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem:
Current demotion/eviction paths for GPU KV shards rely on heuristics tuned for steady-state LRU/TTL mixes. Continuous batching introduces transient working sets and inflight KV lifetimes that break assumptions: aggressive demotion can evict prefixes still referenced by in-flight batched requests, causing correctness/regression in generation (token mismatch) and tail latency spikes when we must recompute KV state.

Goal:
Introduce a lightweight 'safety envelope' and probe-driven demotion protocol that: 1) prevents demotion of prefix slices with active batching references, 2) bounds additional GPU memory reserved for probe metadata, 3) preserves latency SLOs and amortized token cost goals, and 4) provides verifiable correctness invariants for prefix liveness across demotion windows.

Approach (high level):
- Add continuous-batching probes: short-lived, low-overhead markers attached to batches that describe prefix dependencies (prefix IDs, last-accessed seq). Probes are propagated to the KV demotion controller so it can defer demotion for observed prefixes until probes expire or explicit lease drop.
- Safety envelope: a configurable demotion window (microseconds/ms) per prefix cohort computed from observed batch inflight durations + margin. Demotion decisions must respect envelope; if demotion would violate envelope, we either (a) delay demotion, or (b) demote to a compressed/reduced-fidelity representation that is safe for fallback.
- Probe-driven fallback: when memory pressure necessitates reclaiming envelope-protected slots, prefer demoting unprobed prefixes first, then compact probed prefixes (quantized KV) before full eviction.
- Correctness invariants: demotion cannot remove a KV entry that has an outstanding probe referencing a sequence <= probe.seq_max. We will formalize and assert this invariant in unit and integration tests.

Trade-offs considered:
- Reserving probe metadata increases per-GPU memory overhead by ~0.5-2% but prevents costly recompute on eviction.
- Delaying demotion may slightly increase peak memory but reduces tail latency/regeneration cost.
- Compacting KV entries (reduced fidelity) is a middle ground vs full eviction but requires model support for degraded KV reads; we will gate compaction to model families that support it.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Safety+Envelope+for+Demotion
- RFC PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/412
- Spike benchmarks and perf dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/d/kv/demotion-probes-2026-02
- Prototype PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8276

Metrics to track:
- correctness_regressions: token-diff rate on regression suite (target <0.01%)
- tail_latency_99.9: should not increase >5% over baseline
- extra_memory_pct: probe/reservation overhead (target <2%)
- demotion_delay_ms: median and 99th percentile

Rollout plan:
1) Feature-flagged prototype on canary pool (non-production models) with detailed tracing.
2) Extend regression suite to include batched-inflight scenarios and assert invariants.
3) Canary on low-traffic customer workload for 48h.
4) Gradual rollout with telemetry thresholds for auto-rollback.

Open questions:
- What is the safest default demotion window at 8k/16k sequence lengths? (Spike suggests 10ms for short batches, 80ms for long bursts)
- Should compaction be enabled by default or opt-in per model?
- How to expose probe diagnostics in Console without adding noise?
acceptance_criteria: Prototype implements probe metadata propagation and respects safety envelope for demotion decisions
Automated invariants assert no evictions of prefixes with active probes in unit and integration tests
Canary perf shows token-diff regression rate < 0.01% and tail latency increase <= 5%
Telemetry dashboards for demotion_delay_ms, extra_memory_pct, and probe_hit_ratio are live
Design doc updated with fallback compaction details and rollout steps
